sections.title: Mental model — pay log n once, query free forever

blocks.md: Constraint math decides everything: q queries over static array ⇒ rebuild per query dies (q·n); prefix dies only for MIN/MAX; **sparse table** pays Θ(n log n) build then O(1) idempotent queries. Dynamic updates? Different beast (segment trees, later module).
**Static array + many range queries = sparse table. Range updates + point reads = difference array. Window extrema = monotonic deque. Memorize the three pairings.**

items.q: Why does sparse table need IDEMPOTENT operation?
options: overlapping blocks may double-count element — min/max/idempotent-safe; SUM is not
items.explain: Overlap tolerance is the O(1) trick's price.

blocks.label: sliding window maximum (LC239)
blocks.py:
from collections import deque
dq = deque()                      # indices, values DECREASING
ans = []
for i in range(n):
    if dq and dq[0] <= i - k: dq.popleft()    # expired
    while dq and a[dq[-1]] <= a[i]: dq.pop()  # dominated
    dq.append(i)
    if i >= k - 1: ans.append(a[dq[0]])

blocks.md: **Amortized defense:** every index pushed once, popped ≤ once ⇒ O(n) total despite nested whiles. Recite exactly this when challenged.

blocks.md: **LC862 doctrine:** negatives break windows ⇒ move to PREFIX space. Want shortest subarray sum ≥ K: keep prefix indices in deque with INCREASING prefix values; pop-back keeps candidates ascending; pop-front answers while pre[front] ≤ cur − K.

chain.q: Why pop-back when new prefix smaller/equal than back?
chain.a: Any future start using that older-larger prefix is strictly worse (later position, bigger value) — dominated permanently. Monotonicity restored.
Offline arbitrary-range queries without update: sort queries block-wise, amortized O((n+q)√n). Overkill vs sparse table when idempotent — mention as alternative universe.

chain.q: When segment tree replaces all this?
chain.a: Updates interleaved with queries — sparse/diff/deque assume static or batched; tree handles live mutation at log n each. Bridge arrives in Trees/Segment module.

items.title: Sliding Window Maximum
items.statement: Section machinery verbatim; then defend amortized O(n) with push/pop accounting.
hints: Strict vs non-strict pop affects duplicate handling — test equal floods.

solutionCode.label: monotonic deque of indices, decreasing by value

items.complexity: Time O(n) amortised — each index is pushed once and popped once. Space O(k) for the deque.

followups.a: Every index is pushed exactly once. Each pop — front or back — removes an index permanently, so total pops ≤ total pushes = n. The inner while loop can run many times on one iteration but at most n times across the whole scan, giving 2n deque operations overall.

followups.q: Why store indices rather than values, and does `<=` vs `<` matter?
followups.a: Indices are needed to detect expiry (`dq.front() <= i - k`); values alone cannot tell you when an element leaves the window. Using `<=` on the dominated-pop evicts equal values, keeping only the newest duplicate — which is correct and keeps the deque smaller. Strict `<` also yields correct maxima but retains duplicates, so test an all-equal array either way.

items.title: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K
items.statement: Negatives included — the window killer. Implement prefix+deque doctrine.
hints: Pop-back dominated prefixes before pushing i.

solutionCode.label: prefix sums plus an increasing-prefix deque

items.complexity: Time O(n) amortised. Space O(n) for the prefix array and deque.

followups.q: Why does the sliding window from "Minimum Size Subarray Sum" fail here?
followups.a: That window relies on the sum being monotonic in the window bounds, which holds only for non-negative values. With negatives, extending right can decrease the sum, so "shrink while sum ≥ target" no longer safely retires the left edge. Prefix sums plus a deque restores a monotonic structure to search over.

Pop-front: once pre[i] − pre[front] ≥ K, that front gives a valid subarray, and any later i only makes it longer — so record and discard it permanently. Pop-back: if pre[back] ≥ pre[i] with back < i, then i is both a later and a smaller prefix, so it dominates back as a future left endpoint in every way.

items.title: Range Update Drill (diff array)
items.statement: m range-add ops, then q point reads. Materialize once; compare against naive m·range cost aloud.
hints: Endpoint mutations only during op phase.

solutionCode.label: difference array: two writes per range op, one prefix sweep
solutionCode.py:
class DiffArray:
    def __init__(self, n: int):
        self.n = n
        self.d = [0] * (n + 1)

    def range_add(self, l: int, r: int, v: int) -> None:   # inclusive [l, r]
        self.d[l] += v
        self.d[r + 1] -= v          # cancel just past the end

    def materialize(self) -> list[int]:                    # call once, after all ops
        out, run = [], 0
        for i in range(self.n):
            run += self.d[i]
            out.append(run)
        return out

items.complexity: Build O(m + n) for m range updates instead of O(m·n) naive. Each point read is O(1) after the sweep.

followups.a: Naive is O(m·n) — with m = n = 2×10^5 that is 4×10^10 writes, hopeless. The difference array does two writes per op plus one linear sweep: O(m + n) ≈ 4×10^5. The catch is that reads are only valid after materialisation, so it fits offline batches, not interleaved read/write traffic.

followups.q: What if updates and queries interleave?
followups.a: A difference array no longer works, because materialising after every update costs O(n). Use a Fenwick tree over the difference array for O(log n) range-update and point-query, or a lazy segment tree for range-update with range-query.

items.title: Static RMQ Battery
items.statement: Build sparse table for n=2×10⁵, answer 2×10⁵ min-queries in O(1). Include __lg log table.

solutionCode.label: sparse table over an idempotent operation

items.complexity: Build O(n log n) time and memory; each query O(1). At n = 2×10^5 the table is n × 18 ints ≈ 14 MB as 32-bit — announce that before allocating.

followups.a: "min is idempotent — min(x, x) = x — so the two covering halves are allowed to overlap without corrupting the answer." That is what buys O(1) queries. Sum is not idempotent, which is why range-sum needs a prefix array or a Fenwick tree instead of a sparse table.

followups.q: Why precompute a log table instead of calling a log function?
followups.a: The query is O(1) only if the log is O(1). Computing lg[i] = lg[i/2] + 1 fills the table in one linear pass and keeps everything in integer arithmetic — no floating-point rounding that could pick the wrong power of two at a boundary.

items.title: Num Matrix — Rectangle Sum Queries
items.statement: Prebuild 2D prefix with padded border; O(1) rect answers; watch off-by-one corners.

solutionCode.label: 2D prefix with a padded border, inclusion-exclusion

items.complexity: Build O(m·n) once; every rectangle query O(1). Space O(m·n).

followups.q: What does the padded border actually buy?
followups.a: It removes every boundary branch. A query touching row 0 or column 0 would otherwise need `r1 == 0 ? 0 : pre[r1][...]` guards on two of the four terms; with a zero border those reads are legal and return 0 naturally.

Start from the big rectangle to (r2,c2). Subtract the strip above and the strip to the left. Their intersection — the top-left block — has now been removed twice, so add it back once. It is inclusion-exclusion on two overlapping half-planes.

items.title: Sum of Subarray Minimums (preview)
items.statement: Contribution technique: each element counted for spans where it's the min. Full stack machinery lands next modules — attempt with hints.
hints: left[i]: distance to previous smaller; right[i]: next smaller-or-equal.

solutionCode.label: contribution technique with a one-side-equal tiebreak
solutionCode.py:
def sum_subarray_mins(a: list[int]) -> int:
    MOD = 1_000_000_007
    n = len(a)
    left, right, st = [0] * n, [0] * n, []

    # left[i]: span using PREVIOUS STRICTLY SMALLER
    for i in range(n):
        while st and a[st[-1]] >= a[i]:
            st.pop()
        left[i] = i + 1 if not st else i - st[-1]
        st.append(i)
    st.clear()
    # right[i]: NEXT SMALLER-OR-EQUAL -- equality lives on exactly one side
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        while st and a[st[-1]] > a[i]:
            st.pop()
        right[i] = n - i if not st else st[-1] - i
        st.append(i)

    return sum(a[i] * left[i] * right[i] for i in range(n)) % MOD

items.complexity: Time O(n) — two monotonic-stack passes. Space O(n).

followups.q: Why must equality be allowed on exactly one side?
followups.a: With duplicates, a subarray whose minimum appears twice would be credited to both occurrences if both sides used non-strict comparisons, double counting it. Making one side strict and the other non-strict assigns each subarray to exactly one representative occurrence — conventionally the leftmost.

followups.q: Where does left[i] * right[i] come from?
followups.a: a[i] is the minimum of every subarray whose left endpoint lies in the left[i] choices reaching back to the previous smaller element, and whose right endpoint lies in the right[i] choices reaching forward to the next smaller. Those choices are independent, so the count multiplies, and each such subarray contributes a[i].
